doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

chapter: Radio, the Jazz Institute and Kenton
title: Kenton's divided audience and Poston's father's tastes
summary: Rowe and Poston discuss how people love or hate Kenton; Poston's father loved swing and Harry James but disliked Kenton, whom Poston met at a clinic.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I found the same thing and I just was finishing a podcast episode about band leaders and I included Mr. Kenton. And in reading it, the dichotomy between people who loved him and people who couldn’t stand his music is really quite amazing. Even sometimes the musicians who played in the band.
Yeah. Stan didn’t swing you know.

No. And there’s not much in between you know it’s either — and I remember my dad, I mean one of the things growing up I think that probably interested me in the music was my dad came from the swing era, and he had all the records and you know he loved the big bands. So I grew up hearing those bands. And when I started to play the trumpet in I don’t know fifth grade, sixth grade, whenever you start doing that, I would — probably to please my dad, not that he insisted on that, but I thought it was fun to — he loved Harry James. I thought it was fun, I would figure out the notes — I didn’t know anything about — I’m in like fifth grade or sixth grade — I didn’t know anything about notation or anything but I would just write down the sequence of notes and I learned to play “You Made Me Love You” and things like that. And my dad would be thrilled you know because I could play his favorite Harry James tune. So I would hear these things. But I remember my dad did not like Stan Kenton. Didn’t have any Stan Kenton records, didn’t like that band at all. And the way I know that is because Stan Kenton, when I was in high school, came around — one of the clinics was at the Kansas City, Kansas Community College. And we got to go out to the clinic. And I was star-struck by all of that, just because, you know here’s Stan Kenton and you kind of get to play with him ‘cause he’s playing the piano while you’re playing. And it was a big deal. I remember thinking what a big deal. And my dad was like aagh, you know, never cared for that. So it’s interesting because he’s very representative of the side that just, you know, has no open mind about it whatsoever you know, it just didn’t swing, didn’t like it.
